abstract: Producing long-form videos from narration requires interdependent decisions that remain coherent across shots. Existing agentic editors often use multi-stage workflows driven by general models, leaving the quality-cost trade-off of compact, task-adapted policies unclear. We address this gap with WeVisCut, a long-form script-to-video system that connects tool execution with policy learning. Its agent harness maintains shared production state so that tool feedback informs subsequent decisions and repairs. Because finished videos do not expose these decisions, our four-stage data pipeline combines editing inversion with verified replay to turn recovered editing intent into executable supervision. Applied to 3,750 finished videos, this pipeline yields over 130K training examples. We use this supervision to train a single 9B policy that coordinates production and recovers from failures within the same harness. Moreover, we introduce a 100-task benchmark and five metrics assessing editing quality and delivery reliability. Under a shared tool environment, WeVisCut substantially outperforms its base model and achieves comparable performance to Claude Opus 5 while using nearly 33$\times$ fewer generated tokens per successful output minute. It also outperforms task-matched native editors on our proposed metrics.

sections.body: Narrated long-form video editing couples planning, visual retrieval, narration synthesis and timeline assembly, so a change to one shot can affect later timestamps. Finished videos omit the tool calls and failures needed for training, so the paper builds a four-stage data pipeline over 3,750 video projects that yields over 130K training examples. A single 9B policy is trained across production roles, and a 100-task benchmark with five metrics evaluates editing quality and delivery reliability. In a shared tool environment, the policy improves its base model by 16.0 points in Overall Score and reaches comparable performance to Claude Opus 5 while using nearly 33$\times$ fewer generated tokens per successful output minute.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: WeVisCut couples a stateful script-to-video harness with executable data and one 9B policy for narrated long-form video.

sections.body: Related work covers three areas. Tool-agent training includes interleaved reasoning, learned API calls, and Guided-OPD, which trains on mixed teacher and student turns. Video editing systems range from user-assisted tools such as LAVE to automated agents such as CutClaw, CineAgents, and Crayotter. Prior task-specific training includes ScripterAgent with a separate DirectorAgent and a 9B policy trained on manually constructed tasks. Evaluation work includes VBench, VideoScore, and Goku-Bench, which assess video quality or instruction-based edits. The paper states that WeVisCut learns one role-routed policy from executable trajectories and links scripts, shot plans, tool trajectories, and rendered videos in one benchmark.
sections.heading: Related Work
sections.headline: Related work contrasts WeVisCut with tool-agent training, video editing agents, and evaluations that do not link scripts, traces, and renders.

sections.body: The task takes a fixed narration script, a target aspect ratio, a feasible duration interval, and a versioned shared tool space, and returns a rendered video, a typed shot plan, and an execution trajectory. One policy with shared parameters serves three roles: the orchestrator selects tools, the generator supplies structured content, and the critic inspects artifacts and requests repairs. The runtime validates each action against its tool contract and commits only validated results to the production state, while rejected calls return typed blockers. Quality inspection combines structured checks with a VLM-Judge over spotlight renders, and repair tools recheck affected artifacts while keeping still-valid results. Repair attempts are bounded, and a run without a validated final video is recorded as incomplete.
sections.heading: WeVisCut Agent Framework
sections.headline: A shared policy chooses tools over a stateful runtime that validates calls, keeps artifacts, and repairs shots before delivery.

sections.body: The source data are 3,750 finished narration-driven video projects collected from Bilibili across four domains. Editing inversion recovers timestamped narration, shot structure, and sentence-shot alignment, which describes intended video structure rather than the original editor's tool actions. Verified replay executes that intent with schema-checked tools and checks asset references, audio durations, and rendered outputs against the artifacts actually produced. Observe-reflect-repair applies bounded local repairs while preserving successful artifacts. Trajectory materialization keeps missing arguments and failed delivery checks visible rather than rewriting them as successes. The split is by source project and yields 134,771 examples.
sections.heading: Data Construction
sections.headline: Four-stage pipeline recovers editing intent from finished videos and replays it to produce executable training examples.

sections.body: Phase 1 trains Qwen3.5-9B with LoRA on the 134,771 examples, computing the loss only on model response tokens, and adds runtime-verified rejection-sampled fine-tuning. At the first recoverable failure, the last replayable state is restored and the teacher regenerates the remaining sequence. Phase 2 applies Guided-OPD on policy-reached states. At each training update, the teacher generates a complete role output with probability $\beta_{n}$ and the student generates it otherwise, and $\beta_{n}$ is gradually reduced to zero. Phase 3 applies RCF-DAPO, which compares candidate outputs only within matched roles and contexts and normalizes rewards within each group. The Guided-OPD and RCF-DAPO configurations are given in an appendix table.
sections.heading: Training WeVisCut
sections.headline: Three phases train the policy by imitation, recovery learning on policy-reached states, and decision optimization within matched roles.

sections.body: Experiments use 100 held-out tasks, five independent runs, and five metrics: script fidelity (SCF), visual-narration semantic match (VNSM), timeline plan realization (TPR), long-horizon consistency (LHC), and end-to-end rendering yield (ERY). In the shared tool environment, WeVisCut raises its Qwen3.5-9B initialization from 74.5 to 90.5 Overall Score, with all five metrics improving. It scores 90.5 against 89.9 for Claude Opus 5, using 2,377 generated tokens per successful output minute versus 78,763. Phase 3 alone raises Overall Score from 84.9 to 90.5. In blinded human ratings by three annotators, overall preference is 4.56 for WeVisCut, 3.48 for Crayotter, and 3.46 for VideoAgent. The authors note these descriptive means do not establish statistical significance.
sections.heading: Experiments
sections.headline: On 100 held-out tasks, WeVisCut reaches 90.5 Overall Score, close to Claude Opus 5 at 89.9, with far fewer generated tokens.

sections.body: The paper presents WeVisCut, a long-form script-to-video system built around one 9B policy shared by the orchestrator, generator, and critic roles. Its four-stage pipeline recovers executable supervision from finished videos, and its 100-task benchmark links scripts, plans, traces, and videos through five metrics. The trained policy improves all five metrics over its base model and approaches Claude Opus 5 while using approximately one thirty-third as many generated tokens per successful output minute. Native-system comparisons and blinded human ratings also favor WeVisCut. The authors state that broader template coverage and stronger retrieval are needed to extend the system to a wider range of editing tasks.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: The trained 9B policy improves all five metrics over its base model and approaches Claude Opus 5 at lower generation cost.

sections.body: The appendix gives the replay admission checks for recovered failures and the Guided-OPD loss, which uses truncated forward KL on teacher outputs and reverse KL on student outputs. It specifies the cosine intervention schedule, a 50-call horizon for Guided-OPD, and a 16-call deployment budget for RL. It defines RCF-DAPO rewards for each role, with six rule features weighted 0.353, 0.186, 0.179, 0.144, 0.081, and 0.057. It also states the evaluation protocol, a baseline task-contract audit, a failure-rate diagnostic, and a sample production trace. Stated limitations include the HyperFrames template library, dataset coverage, retriever stability, and possible judge bias in the VLM-based VNSM evaluation.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix lists admission rules for replayed training data, loss and intervention schedules, reward formulas, evaluation protocol, and a sample trace.
